name: Chapter 2: The first trade
description: The learner makes the first trade and sees that the price is just the last trade.

lesson.title: The first trade
lesson.summary: Place the market's first order yourself and see where 'the price' comes from: it is simply the last trade, not a measure of what the company is worth.

beats.title: A market with no price
beats.text:
The market maker is quoting 99.90 bid and 100.10 ask, with more behind each.

The chart is still empty: there is no price until someone actually trades.

beats.title: Your first order
beats.text: Place the market's first order yourself: [b]buy 10 shares at market[/b]. A market order takes the best price available right now, whatever it is.

wait.hint: In the order ticket choose Buy, Market, quantity 10, then Submit order. Or press Do it for me.

beats.title: Let it trade
beats.text: Your order is queued at the exchange. Nothing happens until the simulation moves forward.

wait.hint: Press Step until your order trades (or Tick to do it all at once).

beats.title: That trade is now the price
beats.text:
You bought at [b]100.10[/b], the market maker's ask. That single trade is now 'the price': the chart shows it and the last price reads 100.10.

Nothing about the company changed. One trade simply happened at that number.

beats.title: The price drops, with no news
beats.text:
Harbor Pension Fund sells 5 shares at market. They trade at the best bid, [b]99.90[/b], and the price 'falls' by 0.20.

The company is exactly the same as a moment ago. The last price moved only because the last trade happened on the other side of the spread.

beats.title: What 'the price' means
beats.text:
The quoted price is just the last trade. With a wide spread it bounces between bid and ask without any news at all.

Remember this for later chapters: whoever controls [i]where[/i] trades happen controls 'the price'.
